topComments.author: AnimalMuppet
topComments.text: There are two issues: 1) transitioning your skills, and 2) persuading someone to hire/pay you for your new skills. Transitioning your skills is possible. But embedded is a different world and a different mindset. You a lot less RAM and a smaller CPU. You may have hard deadlines - the right answer can be wrong if it's too late. You may have multiple threads that have to share data and not corrupt it, no matter what order events occur in. In the worst case, you may not have logging available at all, and you may not have a debugger. (I think the worst I ever had to do was attach a logic analyzer to the address bus, triggered by a specific address, and then use it to look at past memory addresses in order to figure out what path of execution had got me to the point of the crash.) So, yeah. It's a different world. Learnable, but different. Getting someone to believe you can do it enough that they're willing to pay you: I don't have great advice there. I spent almost my whole career in embedded. It seems to me that it's easier to get from there into, say, desktop programming, than it is to go the other way. In general Pi-s are relatively bad for timekeeping. Not just the NIC (which can be replaced by hats with their own), there are also oscillator replacement mods[2] to work around this to some extent. So if the goal is low-cost precise timekeeping, one can assemble something FPGA-based[2] for quite a bit less money, that can reach very low noise figures. You can spend the remaining money on the GNSS antenna and receiver instead. topComments.text: I think the future of hard drives involves absolutely huge error correction block sizes - 1 gigabyte or more. The way it would work is: * The underlying disk would do sequential writes only, in 1Gb blocks, rather like a log filesystem. * The large block size enables much better information density due to being able to tolerate far more errors. * Random reads within blocks can usually be done - but occasionally most or all of the whole block will need to be read to decode the data. * A small capacitor+disk momentum ensures any writes that happened before a power failure can always be completed - either to the real disk or to flash. * The OS still only sees 4k pages - versioning, packing those into 1Gb blocks, mappings and garbage collection are all handled inside the drive.

stackOverflowQuestions.title: Reliably finding and screenshotting Windows 11 XAML context menus (PopupHost) with pywinauto / UIA?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I'm trying to automate taking cropped screenshots of Windows 11 UI steps (context menus, Run dialog, Registry Editor, Task Manager) using Python ( pywinauto with backend="uia" , pyautogui , and mss ). The script works fine on classic Win32 dialogs, but it breaks constantly on Windows 11's newer XAML / WinUI 3 surfaces: On the new right-click context menu ( PopupHost ), Desktop(backend="uia") either times out traversing the tree or returns stale coordinates, and the menu immediately closes if anything steals focus. Using pygetwindow.getActiveWindow() + mss often captures the underlying Explorer window instead of the popup menu or modal dialog. As a workaround I tried overlaying a 200px coordinate grid on full-screen captures and using visual detection/OCR instead of UIA, which works around the tree hangs, but still feels fragile for small menu items. Here is the simplified capture + UIA lookup I started with: import time import pyautogui from pywinauto import Desktop pyautogui.rightClick(500, 300) time.sleep(0.5) desktop = Desktop(backend="uia") # Often hangs or misses "Show more options" inside Win11 XAML context menu popup = desktop.window(class_name="PopupHost") item = popup.child_window(title="Show more options", control_type="MenuItem") rect = item.rectangle() Is there a reliable way in Python to query bounding boxes of Windows 11 XAML popups (like PopupHost ) without hanging UIA or dismissing the menu? Or is calling the Windows UI Automation COM API directly (e.g., via comtypes / uiautomation ) significantly more stable than pywinauto for WinUI 3?
